q: When a capacitor is connected to a battery, the two conductors have charges of equal magnitude and opposite signs.
e: True. A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy and holds a pd at its terminals. Battery, the two conductors have charges of equal magnitude and opposite signs.

q: The magnitude of the charge on each conductor, Q, is called the potential difference of the capacitor.
e: False. The right claim is this: The magnitude of the charge Q on each conductor is called the charge of the capacitor. Two conductors and a dielectric hold opposite charge, so energy sits in the electric field. The printed line wrongly says the magnitude of the charge on each conductor, Q, is called the potential difference of the capacitor.

q: The potential difference between two conductors of the capacitor, V, is called the potential difference of the capacitor.
e: True. A conductor lets charge drift when a potential difference is applied across it. Of the capacitor, V, is called the potential difference of the capacitor.

q: The quantity of charge Q on the capacitor is inversely proportional to the potential difference V between the conductors.
e: False. The right claim is this: The quantity of charge Q on the capacitor is linearly proportional to the potential difference V between the conductors. A conductor lets charge drift when a potential difference is applied across it. The printed line wrongly says the quantity of charge Q on the capacitor is inversely proportional to the potential difference V between the conductors.

q: The relationship between charge and potential difference can be written as $Q = CV$.
e: True. Potential difference is the electrical push between two points; no push, no current. The relation in this line is Q = CV.

q: The capacitance of a capacitor is defined as the product of the charge and the potential difference of the capacitor.
e: False. The right claim is this: The capacitance of a capacitor is defined as the ratio of the charge to the potential difference of the capacitor. Potential difference is the electrical push between two points; no push, no current. The printed line wrongly says the capacitance of a capacitor is defined as the product of the charge and the potential difference of the capacitor.

q: The capacitance is represented as $C = \frac{Q}{V}$.
e: True. This capacitance is represented as C = (Q)/(V). The relation in this line is C = (Q)/(V).

q: In the SI system, the unit of capacitance is the coulomb.
e: False. The right claim is this: In the SI system, the unit of capacitance is the farad. One farad is one coulomb per volt, so practical capacitors are µF, nF or pF. The printed line wrongly says in the SI system, the unit of capacitance is the coulomb.

q: If the potential difference of the capacitor is 1 V when it is given a charge 1 C, its capacitance is 1 F.
e: True. Charge is conserved; it is what a current carries and what a capacitor stores on its plates. The value 1 V is the figure this statement is using.

q: The unit farad is named in honor of Isaac Newton.
e: False. The right claim is this: The unit farad is named in honor of Michael Faraday. Faraday's law: induced emf equals the rate of change of magnetic flux through the loop. The printed line wrongly says the unit farad is named in honor of Isaac Newton.

q: The farad is a very small unit of capacitance.
e: False. The right claim is this: The farad is a very large unit of capacitance. One farad is one coulomb per volt, so practical capacitors are µF, nF or pF. The printed line wrongly says the farad is a very small unit of capacitance.

q: 1 microfarad ($\mu$F) is equal to $10^{-6}$ F.
e: True. A microfarad is 10^-6 F, the usual electrolytic size. The power 10^-6 is the conversion for this unit; a nearby prefix is a different size.

q: 1 nanofarad (nF) is equal to $10^{-12}$ F.
e: False. The right claim is this: 1 nanofarad (nF) is equal to 10^-9 F. A nanofarad is 10^-9 F, a thousand times smaller than a microfarad. The printed line wrongly says 1 nanofarad (nF) is equal to 10^-12 F.

q: 1 picofarad (pF) is equal to $10^{-12}$ F.
e: True. A picofarad is 10^-12 F, the small ceramic and stray-capacitance scale. The power 10^-12 is the conversion for this unit; a nearby prefix is a different size.

q: When the charge on the capacitor is increased, the potential difference decreases proportionally.
e: False. The right claim is this: When the charge on the capacitor is increased, the potential difference also increases proportionally. Charge is conserved; it is what a current carries and what a capacitor stores on its plates. The printed line wrongly says when the charge on the capacitor is increased, the potential difference decreases proportionally.

q: The capacitance of a capacitor remains constant when the charge on it is increased.
e: True. Charge is conserved; it is what a current carries and what a capacitor stores on its plates. The capacitance of a capacitor remains constant when the charge on it is increased.

q: The capacitance of a capacitor depends on the magnitude of the charge Q and the potential difference V.
e: False. The right claim is this: If the potential difference of the capacitor is 1 V when it is given a charge 1 C, its capacitance is 1 F. Charge is conserved; it is what a current carries and what a capacitor stores on its plates. The printed line wrongly says the capacitance of a capacitor depends on the magnitude of the charge Q and the potential difference V.

q: The capacitance of a capacitor depends on the size and the shape of the capacitor.
e: True. Two conductors and a dielectric hold opposite charge, so energy sits in the electric field. A capacitor depends on the size and the shape of the capacitor.

q: The capacitance of a capacitor depends on the nature of the insulator between the two conductors.
e: True. An insulator does not let charge flow freely, so it can separate conductors or protect a live part. Capacitor depends on the nature of the insulator between the two conductors.

q: The amount of charge given to a conductor to change its potential by one unit is called the electric capacity of the conductor.
e: True. Charge is conserved; it is what a current carries and what a capacitor stores on its plates. Potential by one unit is called the electric capacity of the conductor.

q: The electric capacity of a conductor is expressed by the equation $C = \frac{V}{Q}$.
e: False. The right claim is this: The amount of charge given to a conductor to change its potential by one unit is called the electric capacity of the conductor. A conductor lets charge drift when a potential difference is applied across it. The printed line wrongly says the electric capacity of a conductor is expressed by the equation C = (V)/(Q).

q: The SI unit of electric capacity of a conductor is the volt.
e: False. The right claim is this: The amount of charge given to a conductor to change its potential by one unit is called the electric capacity of the conductor. Charge is conserved; it is what a current carries and what a capacitor stores on its plates. The printed line wrongly says the SI unit of electric capacity of a conductor is the volt.

q: A capacitor stores charge Q at a potential difference V; if the voltage applied is doubled, the charge is halved.
e: False. The right claim is this: The charge of the equivalent capacitor in series is Q when the total potential difference V is applied. Series capacitors share charge, voltages add, and equivalent C is smaller than the smallest. The printed line wrongly says a capacitor stores charge Q at a potential difference V; if the voltage applied is doubled, the charge is halved.

q: 1 F is equivalent to 1 C V$^{-1}$.
e: True. One farad is one coulomb per volt, so practical capacitors are µF, nF or pF. The value 1 F is the figure this statement is using.

q: Typical devices have capacitances ranging from microfarad ($\mu$F) to picofarad (pF).
e: True. A microfarad is 10^-6 F, the usual electrolytic size. Typical devices have capacitances ranging from microfarad (µF) to picofarad (pF).
